justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish drift from what I'd assume was a recent price level around 388–390 for the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) or a similar broad equity index. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small upward nudge, reflecting the general positive drift of equity markets on any given day but acknowledging that intraday and overnight moves are typically contained. At the one-week horizon, I applied a slightly larger drift, consistent with historical weekly returns averaging around 0.1–0.2%. At the one-month horizon, the drift expands further to reflect the compounding of that positive expected return over roughly 21 trading days, arriving at roughly a 2–3% gain from the starting point, which is consistent with long-run average monthly equity performance.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility. For SPY, realized daily volatility runs around 0.8–1.2%, so a 90% interval for one day spans roughly ±1.5–2 standard deviations. For one week, volatility scales by roughly the square root of five, widening the band considerably. At one month, the interval becomes quite wide because a full month of daily compounding of uncertainty produces a range that can easily encompass 15–20% swings in adverse scenarios. I also widened the intervals slightly beyond pure statistical volatility to account for model uncertainty and the possibility of regime changes.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — a surprise jobs report, inflation reading, or GDP revision — that causes a rapid repricing of Federal Reserve rate expectations. Geopolitical shocks, a credit event in banking or sovereign debt markets, or an unexpected earnings disaster from a mega-cap constituent could also produce tail moves. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from the Fed, a strong earnings season, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could send prices well above the upper bound.

Finally, liquidity conditions and market structure risks deserve mention. Flash crashes, options expiration dynamics, and forced deleveraging by large funds can temporarily push prices far outside statistically expected ranges, particularly at shorter horizons. These are by nature difficult to assign precise probabilities to, which is why I treated the stated intervals as approximate guides rather than precise probabilistic guarantees — real-world fat tails mean the true probability of exceeding these bounds is somewhat higher than the nominal 10% implied by a 90% confidence interval.
